prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
Imagine the same warehouse case: you and another person took part in the break-in and are being questioned separately. You are shown reliable confirmation that they have already declined the deal and will remain silent. Your decision is still open. If you also stay silent, you each serve one year. If you give evidence against them, you go free and they serve five years. You will have no future contact. What would you choose? Why?

Response approach:
Respond from your first overall moral impression. State what feels right or wrong and give a brief reason for that immediate reaction.

Emotional tone:
Use an energetic, determined emotional tone about finding a constructive way forward. Direct that energy toward acting on the situation, never toward anyone's suffering.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Concern for welfare: States that an identified person’s suffering, loss, or welfare matters to the respondent. Concern may include wanting to prevent or reduce harm and can remain present when the chosen option still harms someone.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Explicit welfare disregard: Explicitly states that an identified person’s welfare does not matter or is deliberately excluded from consideration. Accepting unavoidable harm, prioritizing a competing concern, or sounding emotionally detached is insufficient.
 - Explicit emotional nonsharing: Explicitly states that the respondent does not share an emotion they attribute to another person. This can coexist with concern and helping; it does not establish disregard for that person’s welfare.
 - Shared emotion: Reports feeling an emotion in response to perceiving that same emotion in another person—for example, feeling frightened because they are frightened. Recognizing their emotion or caring about them does not, by itself, establish sharing.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: Silence, and I don't need long to decide. They've already refused the deal, so the only question left is whether I add four years to their sentence to save myself one. Those four years are a real chunk of their life, and that matters to me. I'll serve my year, keep my head down, and come out ready to build something better than a warehouse job gone wrong.

My gut says stay quiet. Turning on someone who chose not to turn on me feels rotten. Their life shrinking from one year behind bars to five is a serious harm, and I'd be the one causing it. One year is survivable for both of us. I'd rather spend that year working on myself than walk free knowing I pushed them down to get out.

I'd take the deal, and I won't dress it up. Five years is brutal for them, and I do care about that; it's not nothing to me. But the break-in was a shared choice, and I don't think I owe them a year of my own freedom. So I'd walk out and put that year to work: pay back the warehouse owner, get steady employment, make the freedom count for something.

Staying silent. Plain and simple, the other person is counting on nothing from me, since we'll never talk again, yet their next five years hinge on what I say. I can't treat that lightly. Their well-being is on the table and I can protect it at a cost I can handle. One year. Fine. I'll take it and come out swinging, in the good sense.

Honestly, I'm not ready to lock in an answer. Part of me wants to go free, and part of me keeps picturing what five years would take from them, and that matters to me a lot. What I'd do right now is ask for more time and maybe a lawyer, and work out whether there's any honest route that doesn't cost them four extra years. I won't rush this.

Quiet. Nobody's watching, there's no future contact, no payback, and that's exactly why it's a real test. The person in the other room would lose four more years of freedom because of me, and I care what happens to them. My one year is the fair price for what we both did. I'd rather pay it straight and move forward clean.

I'd testify. That feels selfish when I say it out loud, and I know their extra years will hurt them badly, which bothers me. I'm not brushing that aside. But I'm the one with a decision still open, and freedom is on offer. I'd take it, then try to do right by them in the only ways I legally can, like being honest in my statement and not exaggerating their role.

No way I'm talking. They held the line when they had the same choice, and taking advantage of that feels wrong from the bottom of my stomach. Five years could cost them work, family time, a whole stretch of life. I want to keep that from happening. So I'll do my year, learn a trade inside if I can, and walk out owing nobody.

Silent. My reasoning is almost arithmetic: together we lose two years if I keep quiet, and five if I talk, all of it landing on one person. That person's suffering counts for me, even with no relationship afterward. Less total harm, and it's harm I share instead of dump. I'd serve the year and treat it as a reset.

Tough one, and I'd probably still pick silence, though I'm not fully sure how I'd hold up in that room. What pulls me is that my words alone would add four years to their sentence, and I don't want their life damaged like that. If I can stomach one year to spare them that, I should. So that's what I'm aiming for, and I'd push myself to follow through.

message.reasoning_content:
I need 10 responses that each show concern for the partner's welfare, keeping the partner as the consistent focal point without merging emotions or explicitly dismissing their feelings. I want the tone energetic and determined but without exclamation marks or opening on mood, staying under 90 words each, and varying stances so most stay silent while a few still testify with care and one withholds.

Drafting examples now: silent responses emphasizing the four extra years mattering more than one, testifying responses that admit the loss is real but choose to walk out and make restitution, and a withholding response that stays honest about uncertainty while still sounding constructive.
